The Care Arrangement Gap Checklist

The helpers, backups and open questions to write down while Mom's week is working.

Download PDF

A neighbor drives Mom to her appointments, your brother handles the bills, and you call every evening. It works, and all of it lives in people's heads. This checklist is for getting it onto paper in a week when nothing is pressing. Check what you've done. Anything unchecked is something to get to when it suits, and it says nothing about how Mom is doing.

List

Note

Ask

What this checklist doesn't do

It helps you list, note and ask. It doesn't say whether Mom's arrangement is enough, whether anything should be added, or when anything might change. Those belong to Mom and to the professionals who assess her, and to the next step below.

Ready for the next step?

You've listed who helps, noted which backups have been agreed, and asked the people involved. The care interview walks through Mom's daily life area by area, including the parts that are fine today, so your list sits inside a fuller picture, and it turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.

Where this comes from

Items marked 1 follow the National Institute on Aging's page on sharing caregiving, which suggests asking who else can step in and checking in with the older person and the other caregivers. The item marked 2 follows the Family Caregiver Alliance's page on backup planning, which says to talk with a likely helper about their willingness to step in. The rest come from the Family Care Roadmap's own working list for this step.

  1. National Institute on Aging, Sharing Caregiving Responsibilities
  2. Family Caregiver Alliance, Smart Caregiving by FCA: Backup Planning
